en: The Biography of the Dharma Master Vasubandhu,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
As for the Dharma Master Vasubandhu, he was a native of Puruṣapura in Northern India.
Furthermore,
*Puruṣa* is translated as "Great Man" (*zhàngfū*), and *pura* is translated as "land" (*tǔ*).
Regarding the celestial king Vaiśravaṇa, it is said in the world-transmission (*shìchuán*) that:
This was the younger brother of Śakra; Śakra dispatched him to Jambudvīpa to act as king for the purpose of subduing the asuras.
Born in Jambudvīpa as the son of King Vasudeva, there were asuras [who opposed him].
It is named Indradamana. "Indra" is a name for Śakra;
"damana" is translated as "subduing."
This asura constantly engages in battle with Śakra;
he is given this name because he is able to subdue Śakra.
According to the Vyākaraṇa treatises, "asura" is explained as meaning "one who does not sport well."
One should therefore translate it by this name.
The various devas constantly take what is good as their play and delight;
because they constantly take what is evil as their play and delight, they have this name.
They are also called "Non-Gods" (asura).
This asura has a younger sister named Pāṭalī;
"pāṭa" is translated as "light."
*Bādi* is translated as "consort.
This woman possessed an exceptionally beautiful form.
The Asuras desired to harm the god Viṣṇu.
Therefore, she will deceive him by using her power of incantations to transform a region of Jambudvīpa into darkness;
dwelling herself in this place of gloom, she will ensure that no one can see her.
She sent her younger sister to live in a place of learning and said to her, "If anyone wishes to take you as his wife,
you should tell them that my brother possesses great power."
"If you wish to take me, it must be against my brother's will;
only if you can bring my brother to battle may I grant you my consent.
Later, the god Viśvānara saw this woman at a place of light.
Her heart was greatly delighted,
and she asked, "Who are you?
She replied, "I am an asura maiden."
The Deva said, "All the asura women have traditionally been married to the devas.
Since I have no wife and you have no husband, I wish to take you as my consort; would you grant me your consent?"
The woman answered him with words consistent with what her brother had previously said.
The deva said, "Because you now cherish my body, you have spoken these words.
Since you already love me, how could I possibly abandon you?"
"I possess great power and am able to fight with your elder brother.
The woman then consented, and they immediately became husband and wife.
Later, the asura went to inquire of the god Viṣṇu.
"How is it that you have taken my sister as your wife without permission?
The deity replied, "If I were not a man,
taking your sister as my wife would indeed deserve reproach."
"I am a man without a wife, and your sister is a maiden without a husband.
That I should now take her is precisely what is right; why do you find it strange?
The asura said, 'What ability do you have to claim for yourself the title of a man?'"
"If you, a man of valor, can defeat me in combat, I shall give my younger sister to you as a wife.
The Deva said, "If you do not believe me, let us settle this by a duel.
Thereupon, each took up arms and they struck and pierced one another.
The god Viṣṇu possesses the body of Nārāyaṇa, which weapons cannot penetrate;
when the gods strike off the heads of the asuras, they immediately rejoin,
and it is the same for their arms and all other limbs.
Wherever they are severed, they immediately regenerate.
From morning until evening, they are hacked and pierced without ceasing;
yet the asuras show no signs of death.
When his celestial power was somewhat exhausted, he became weary;
if it reached night, the power of the asuras would become even stronger.
The consort feared that her husband might not prevail.
He took an *utpala* flower, split it into two pieces, and threw each piece to one side.
As the consort walked back and forth between them, the deva immediately understood her intention;
he seized the asura’s body, split it into two pieces, and threw each piece to one side.
The gods, having departed from within it, returned once more.
Because of this, the asuras' lives were cut short.
Previously, the asuras had petitioned the rishis for grace, wishing that their bodies might be restored immediately after being hacked and pierced.
Because the seer had bestowed this kindness upon him, he did not lose his life even when later subjected to hacking and stabbing.
However, because the seer intended for the devas to kill him, he did not bestow the grace of restoring his split body back to its original state.
Consequently, at a later time, he lost his life because of this.
Since the deva Viṣṇu resided in this land and manifested the prowess of a great man (*puruṣa*),
it was for this reason that the name "Land of Men" (*Puruṣabhūmi*) was established.
In this land, there was a state preceptor, a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan,
who had three sons all named Vasubandhu;
"Vasu" is translated as "Heaven."
"Bhandu" is translated as "kinsman.
In India, when naming children, there is this convention:
although they may share the same name, another distinct name is established to clarify their identity.
The third son, Vasubandhu,
entered the monastic order in the Sarvāstivāda school and attained the fruit of arhatship;
he was also known by the alternative name of Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja.
*Pilindavatsa* is his mother’s name;
*vatsa* is translated as "son" or "child.
This name is used for both humans and animals; for instance, the calf of an ox is also called *vatsa*.
In this land, however, the term for a calf is *du* (犢), while the term for an eldest son is *changzi* (長子).
Vasubandhu was a person of bodhisattva lineage;
he also went forth as a monk in the Sarvāstivāda school.
Later, although he cultivated meditative concentration and attained freedom from desire,
he was unable to enter into the realization of the meaning of emptiness through contemplation.
He then desired to take his own life.
The Arhat Piṇḍola,
observing this matter from Pūrvavideha in the east, came from that direction to preach the contemplation of emptiness according to the Hīnayāna.
By contemplating according to the instructions, one immediately attains entry.
Although one has attained the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Hīnayāna, the mind remains unsettled;
thinking that the principle should not stop at this, one proceeds by means of the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of this vehicle.
He went to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult with Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva expounded for him the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness.
Upon returning to Jambudvīpa, he contemplated it exactly as he had been taught.
Even though he attained awakening during the stage of contemplation, when the earth shook in six ways, and having thereby attained the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness,
he was named Asaṅga on account of this.
Asaṅga was translated as "The Unattached.
Thereafter, he ascended several times to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya regarding the meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Maitreya explained them extensively for him, and Asaṅga attained realization accordingly.
Returning to Jambudvīpa,
he explained what he had heard to others; however,
most who heard it did not give rise to faith.
Dharma Master Asaṅga then made this vow:
"I now wish to cause sentient beings to have faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna.
I pray only that the Great Master will descend to Jambudvīpa to explain the Mahāyāna, so that all sentient beings may attain faith and understanding."
Maitreya then, in accordance with that wish, descended to Jambudvīpa during the night.
Emitting a great radiance, he gathered a vast assembly of those with the karmic affinity,
and in the Hall of Dharma Exposition, he recited the *Saptadaśabhūmi-sūtra*.
As each passage was recited, he explained its meaning accordingly.
It was only after four months that his exposition of the *Saptadaśabhūmika-sūtra* was completed.
Although they were listening to the Dharma together in the same hall, [the master’s teaching continued].
Only the Dharma Master Asanga was able to draw near to Maitreya Bodhisattva;
others could only hear him from afar at night as they listened together to Maitreya’s preaching of the Dharma.
During the day, the Dharma Master Asanga would further explain to the others what Maitreya had taught.
Therefore, having heard and believed in the Mahāyāna teachings of Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Dharma Master Asaṅga cultivated the *sūryaprabha-samādhi*.
By practicing and training according to the instructions, he immediately attained this samādhi; from the moment he attained it...
Thereafter, he was able to thoroughly penetrate all that he had previously failed to understand;
whatever he saw or heard, he remembered forever without forgetting.
He fully comprehended the meaning of all the Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the *Avataṃsaka*, which the Buddha had taught in the past.
In the Tuṣita Heaven,
Maitreya expounded the meanings of all the Mahāyāna sūtras for the Dharma Master Wu-zhuo (Asaṅga).
The Dharma Master thoroughly mastered them all and was able to retain them all in memory.
Later, in Jambudvīpa, he composed Mahāyāna sūtra-upadeśas (commentaries) to explain all the great teachings spoken by the Buddha.
The second was Vasubandhu.
He also entered the monastic order in the Sarvāstivāda school.
He was profoundly learned and widely erudite, thoroughly mastering the classical scriptures;
his divine talent and brilliant intelligence were beyond compare.
His moral conduct was so pure and lofty that it was difficult to find his equal.
Since the brothers had distinct names, the Dharma Master was referred to simply as Vasubandhu.
Five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was an Arhat.
His name was Kātyāyanīputra;
he was named after his mother’s clan, Kātyāyana.
He had previously gone forth as a monk in the Sarvāstivāda school.
Originally a native of India, he later went to the kingdom of Kaśmīra,
which lies to the northwest of India. There,
together with five hundred arhats and five hundred bodhisattvas, [he resided].
Together they compiled the Abhidharma of the Sarvāstivāda school,
composing it in eight granthas—
what is here called the eight *piṭakas*.
*Kāṇḍa* is translated as "knot" (*grantha*) or also as "section" (*parvan*).
This is called a "knot" because the various categories of meaning are mutually bound and connected to one another.
Furthermore, it is called a "knot" (*grantha*) because it gathers meanings together so they do not disperse;
it is called a "joint" (*parvan*) because the categories of meaning each have their own limits.

This text is also referred to as a *Prajñā-pradīpa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Arising of Wisdom), for by means of the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the power of vows (*praṇidhāna*), [it brings about wisdom].
He issued a proclamation far and wide:
"If anyone has previously heard the Abhidharma, let them send whatever portions they have obtained, however much or little.
Thereupon, from the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven...
There were among the devas those who had previously heard the Buddha teach the Abhidharma, whether in brief or in detail, even down to a single phrase or a single verse; he sent these all to them.
Kātyāyanīputra, together with the arhats and bodhisattvas, then analyzed and selected their meanings.
If it does not contradict the Sūtras and the Vinaya, one should then compile the inscription;
if it contradicts them, one should discard it.
These selected phrases and sentences are interconnected according to their respective categories of meaning.
If the meaning is "clear wisdom" (*vidyā*), it is placed within the category of wisdom-fetters (*prajñā-saṃyojana*).
If the meaning is "clear concentration" (*samādhi*), it is placed within the category of concentration-fetters.
All other cases are likewise.
The *Aṣṭagrantha* consists of fifty thousand verses.
Having completed the composition of the *Aṣṭagrantha*, he further intended to compose a *Vibhāṣā* commentary upon it.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa was a native of the district of Vākīḍa in Śrāvastī.
He was thoroughly versed in the eightfold Vyākaraṇa,
as well as the four Vedas and the six Śāstras,
and he understood the eighteen schools.
The Tripitaka Master, a paragon of learning and a model for the academy,
was one to whom all turned for guidance. Kātyāyanīputra sent a messenger to Śrāvastī to request Aśvaghoṣa to compose the explanatory prose for the text.
Once Aśvaghoṣa had arrived in Kaśmīra,
Kātyāyanīputra sequentially explained the Eightfold Knots for the sake of the arhats and bodhisattvas.
They then deliberated together on the meaning and intent;
once these were settled, Aśvaghoṣa immediately composed the text.
It took twelve years to complete the *Vibhāṣā*.
There are one million verses in total;
the *Vibhāṣā* translates this as the "Extensive Explanation.
Having completed the exposition:
Kātyāyanīputra immediately set up a stone pillar and inscribed it, saying:
"From this day forth, those who study these various works shall not leave the country of Kaśmīra.
Neither the texts of the *Aṣṭagrantha* nor the texts of the *Vibhāṣā* shall be permitted to leave the country."
Fearing that other schools and the Mahāyāna might defile and corrupt this True Dharma,
they submitted a formal proposal to the King regarding the establishment of regulations;
the King likewise concurred with their intention.
The kingdom of Kaśmīra is surrounded on all sides by mountains like a city wall,
with only a single gate for entry and exit.
The noble ones, through the power of their vows, have summoned yakṣas and deities to guard this gate.
If those who wish to study this Dharma come to Kaśmīra, they shall not be hindered.
Furthermore, by the power of their vows, the noble ones have caused five hundred yakṣas to serve as their patrons (dānapati).
If one studies this Dharma, they will lack nothing for the necessities of life.
In the kingdom of Āyodhyā, there was a Dharma master named Vasubhadra.
Being intelligent and possessed of great wisdom, he was able to retain whatever he heard.
Desiring to study the meaning of the *Aṣṭaskandhaka-vibhāṣā* and propagate it in other lands,
the Dharma Master feigned madness and traveled to the country of Kaśmīra.
He was constantly present in the great assemblies to listen to the Dharma,
yet his deportment was inconsistent and his speech and laughter were discordant;
at times, within those assemblies, he would discuss the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*.
He then asked whether the *Rāmāyaṇa* was known to the people, noting that they held it in low esteem and did not consider it worthy of being recorded.
Over the course of twelve years, he listened to the *Vibhāṣā* until he had mastered its words and meanings through numerous recitations.
Having committed [the teachings] entirely to memory and holding them in his heart, he desired to return to his native land.
As he approached the gate, various yakṣa deities raised their voices and proclaimed:
"The Great Abhidharma Master now wishes to leave the country! They immediately seized him and brought him back to the great assembly.
The assembly collectively interrogated him, but his speech was so incoherent that they could not understand one another.
Everyone considered him a madman and immediately released him.
Later, when the Dharma Master again stepped out the gate, the deities once more shouted for him to be seized and brought back; this report eventually reached the ears of the king.
The king then ordered that he be interrogated again within the great assembly; the multitude interrogated him once more as they had before, yet he remained unintelligible.
This occurred three times in succession.
He departed and returned for a fourth time.
Although the various deities escorted him back, the multitude no longer questioned him;
they ordered the yakṣas to release him and send him out of the country.
Once the Dharma Master had reached his native land, he immediately proclaimed [the news].
"May those both near and far be made to know and hear: I have already mastered the text and meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* of Kaśmīr in its entirety.
Any who are able to study it should come quickly to receive it."
Thereupon, people gathered from the four quarters.

Fearing that his life was waning and he might not be able to complete the exposition of this Dharma, the Dharma Master urged his disciples to take it down quickly as he spoke, writing it down as it emerged; thus, they were able to reach its conclusion.
After the masters of Kaśmīra heard this Dharma, they transmitted it to other lands, where people each marveled at it in admiration.
Nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a non-Buddhist teacher.
It is named Piṇḍārhavaśa; *piṇḍāha* is the name of the mountain, and *vaśa* is translated as "dwelling.
Because these non-Buddhists dwell on this mountain, it is named after them.
There was a nāga king named Vīraśakuna who dwelt in a lake at the foot of Mount Viṃśaka;
this nāga king was well-versed in the Sāṃkhya treatises.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhist practitioners knew that the Dragon King was capable and wished to receive instruction;
thus, the Dragon King transformed his body into the appearance of a rishi and stayed within a leaf hut.
When the non-Buddhists went to the Dragon King's abode, they expressed their intention to study under him.
The Dragon King immediately granted his permission.
The heretic gathered flowers until a large basket was full,
then placed the basket upon his head and went to the place where the Dragon King was.
Each time he circumambulated the Dragon King once, he would immediately cast down a flower as an offering.
With each flower he offered, he composed a verse in praise of the Dragon King;
however, as soon as he heard it, the Dragon King refuted the meaning of the verse he had established.
He immediately took a flower and threw it outside;
once the meaning of the verse he had established according to his offering was established, he threw back the flower he had cast.
In this manner, he threw away an entire basket of flowers until they were exhausted.
The verses that refute the teachings all came before the Dragon King;
having praised his intelligence, he then explained the Sāṃkhya treatises for him, saying: "This is the discourse of the non-Buddhists."
Once you have completed this treatise, be careful not to alter it.
Because the Dragon King fears that it might surpass him, he has caused these [disturbances];
furthermore, the acquisitions resulting from such discernment do not follow a fixed sequence.
If there were passages where the phrasing was not skillful or the meaning was not as intended, he would revise them entirely.
Once the Dragon King had finished his discourse, his composition also concluded;
he then presented the treatise he had written to the Dragon King.
When the Dragon King saw the superior version he had produced,
he was greatly incensed by jealousy and said to the non-Buddhist practitioner,
"I previously instructed you that you must not alter it."
"How can you alter my treatise?
I shall ensure that your composition cannot be circulated.

The non-Buddhist replied, "My teacher originally instructed me that after the treatise was finished, it must not be altered; he did not instruct me that I may not alter it during the course of its exposition."
"I have not disobeyed my teacher's instructions; why then do you reproach me?
I beg my teacher to bestow his grace upon me while my body is still intact;
I pray that you will ensure this treatise does not perish. The teacher then granted him his permission.
After the non-Buddhists obtained this treatise, their minds became haughty and arrogant;
they claimed that their own dharma was supreme and that nothing surpassed it,
except for the Dharma of Śākyamuni, which was flourishing in the world.
Sentient beings claim that this dharma is great;
I must refute it.
He then entered the kingdom of Āyodhyā and struck the drum of debate to proclaim his arguments, saying:
"I wish to debate on the principles of doctrine;
if I fall into defeat, my head shall be cut off, and if he falls into defeat, he shall forfeit his head.
King Bimbisāra Ājātaśatru [agreed].
It was translated as "Zhengle" (Correctly Restrained).
Upon learning of this matter, the king immediately summoned the non-Buddhist practitioners and questioned them.
The non-Buddhists replied, "The King is the sovereign of the nation."
I harbor no partiality toward śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas;
rather, whatever practices they may cultivate, I should test them for their rightness or wrongness.
Now I wish to decide between the superiority and inferiority of myself and the disciples of the Śākya.
"You must swear an oath upon your head.
The king immediately granted permission and dispatched messengers to inquire among the various Dharma masters within the realm:
"Who is capable of confronting this non-Buddhist?"
If there were anyone capable of engaging in debate on the principles of doctrine,
at that time the masters Manoratha and Vasubandhu Dharma Master and others [were present].
All the great Dharma masters had gone to other countries and were not present.
Maṇḍala-ta is translated as "heart-vow."
Only the Dharma Master Vasubandhu and the Dharma Master Buddhamitra were present.
As for Buddhamitra:
He was translated as Jueqin (覺親).
Although this Dharma Master possessed great understanding by nature, he was already advanced in years;
his spirit and faculties were dim and weak, and his eloquence was feeble and faint.
The Dharma Master said, "My great generals of the Dharma are all currently on the field.
Since these arrogant heretics must not be allowed to run rampant,
I myself should now take charge of this matter."
The Dharma Master then informed the king.
The king accordingly set a date and assembled a great multitude at the Hall of Discourse,
ordering the non-Buddhists to debate the Dharma with the Dharma Master.
The non-Buddhist asked, "Does the śramaṇa wish to establish his own tenets, or does he wish to refute those of others?
The Dharma Master replied, "I am like the great ocean, which has nothing it will not contain;
you are like a clod of earth that sinks as soon as it enters it."
"According to your pleasure," the non-Buddhist said,
"O śramaṇa, you may establish a thesis and I shall refute it.
The Dharma Master then established the thesis of impermanence, saying:
All conditioned phenomena perish moment by moment. Why?
Because they are not perceived later.
This is established through various logical principles; such is what the Dharma Master has taught.
Upon hearing it once, the non-Buddhist practitioner could recite it all from memory.
The non-Buddhist then proceeded to refute it point by point using logical reasoning,
causing the Dharma Master to attempt to recite it back but unable to do so.
He commanded the Dharma Master to save him, but the Master was unable to do so;
thus, the Master immediately incurred defeat.
The non-Buddhist said, "You are of the Brahmin caste, and I am also of the Brahmin caste; it is not permissible for you to kill me."
"You must now have your back whipped to demonstrate my victory.
Thereupon, he carried out that act.
The king rewarded the non-Buddhist ascetic with three *lakṣas* of gold.
The non-Buddhist practitioner took gold and scattered it throughout the kingdom as alms for all people;
then, returning to Mount Piṇḍāra, he entered a stone cave and,
through the power of incantations, summoned a yakṣī goddess named Gahvara.
He then entreated the goddess for grace, praying that after his death his body might be transformed into stone and never perish.
The goddess immediately granted his request.
He himself blocked the cave with stone and passed away within it, whereupon his body immediately turned into stone.
The reason he made this vow was that he had previously requested a boon from his teacher, the Dragon King.
"May the Sāṃkhya treatises I have composed not perish before my own body decays.
For this reason, these treatises remain extant even to this day.
Later, when Vasubandhu heard of these matters, he sighed with deep regret and resentment.
He was unable to encounter him.
He dispatched men to Mount Piṇḍava to seek out this non-Buddhist practitioner,
intending to subdue his arrogance and thereby avenge the humiliation of his teacher.
The body of the non-Buddhist had already turned to stone;
Vasubandhu was even more indignant and immediately composed the *Saptati-tattva-śāstra* to refute the *Sāṃkhya-śāstra* produced by the non-Buddhists.
From beginning to end, it collapses like a crumbling wall, with not a single sentence that can stand.
The various non-Buddhists are filled with grief and suffering as if their own lives were being destroyed;
though they did not encounter that Master himself, his *siddhānta* having been ruined, its branches and details have likewise perished.
Having no further basis for existence,
his vengeance was settled and his disgrace washed away here;
all the people heard this and were filled with joy.
The king rewarded the Dharma Master with three *lakṣas* of gold.
The Dharma Master divided this gold into three portions and established three monasteries in the kingdom of Āyodhyā.
First, a bhikṣuṇī monastery;
second, a Sarvāstivāda monastery;
third, a Mahāyāna monastery.
After that, the Dharma Master further established the True Dharma; having first mastered the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*, he subsequently lectured on the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* for the multitude.
On each day of his lectures, he would compose a verse to summarize the meaning taught during that day.
This verse was engraved upon a sheet of red copper and placed beneath the head of an intoxicated elephant, while a drum was beaten to proclaim the command:
"Whoever is able to refute the meaning of this verse, let such a person come forward."
In this manner, he composed more than six hundred verses that encapsulate the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*;
every single one of them is exactly like this.
Consequently, no one was able to refute them; these are the verses of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
After the verse was finished, he sent fifty *kārṣāpaṇas* of gold along with this verse to the various *Vibhāṣā* masters of Kaśmīra.
Upon seeing and hearing it, they were greatly delighted, saying, "Our True Dharma has now been widely propagated."
However, as the verses were profound and abstruse, he could not fully understand them.
Furthermore, he offered fifty *jin* of gold— bringing his previous gift of fifty *jin* to a total of one hundred *jin*— as a tribute to the Dharma Master,
requesting that the Master provide a prose commentary on the meaning of these verses.
The Dharma Master then provided a prose commentary on the verses;
he established the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school, while refuting any erroneous points therein with the tenets of the Sautrāntika school.
This work is titled the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
After the treatise was completed, it was sent to the various masters of Kaśmīra.
Upon seeing that their own tenets were undermined, they each gave rise to grief and suffering.
At that time, King Vikramāditya had a crown prince named Balāditya.
"P'o-lo" is translated as "New," and "Chai-ti-ya" is translated as "Sun.
The King originally ordered the Crown Prince to receive the precepts from the Dharma Master.
The queen consort also left the household life to become a disciple of the Dharma Master.
Later, when the prince ascended the throne, the mother and son together requested that the Dharma Master remain in the kingdom of Āyodhyā to receive their offerings.
The Dharma Master immediately granted his consent.
The Brahmin named Vasurendra, the brother-in-law of King Śrīharṣa,
was a non-Buddhist Dharma master who was learned in the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra.
When Vasubandhu composed the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*,
a non-Buddhist used the principles of the *Vyākaraṇa* (grammar) to refute the textual formulations established by the Dharma Master,
claiming they contradicted the *Vyākaraṇa* and demanding that the Master defend them.
"If we cannot defend this treatise, it will be ruined.
The Dharma Master said, "If I do not understand the Vyākaraṇa, how could I possibly understand its profound meaning?
Nevertheless, the Dharma Master composed a treatise to refute the Vyākaraṇa in thirty-two chapters, destroying it from beginning to end.
Consequently, the Vyākaraṇa treatises were lost,
and only this treatise remained.
The king offered one *lohāṣṭa* (one *loha*) of gold to the Dharma Master.
The Queen Mother offered two *lohāsas* of gold to the Dharma Master.
The Master divided this gold into three portions and established one monastery each in the kingdoms of Puruṣapura, Kaśmīra, and Ādhiṣṭhāna.
Furthermore, these non-Buddhists, feeling shame and indignation and desiring to subdue the Dharma Master,
dispatched a messenger to India to invite the Dharma Master Saṃghabhadra to come to the kingdom of Āryadeśa to compose a treatise refuting the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Upon his arrival, this Dharma Master immediately composed two treatises.
The first was the *Prabhāsa-samayārtha-śāstra*, consisting of ten thousand verses,
which exclusively expounds the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*.
Samaya is translated as "categories of meaning.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* consists of one hundred and twenty thousand verses;
it rescues the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* and refutes the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
After the treatise was completed, he summoned Vasubandhu to debate and resolve the points face-to-face. Vasubandhu,
knowing that although [Saṃghabhadra] had refuted him, he could not destroy the meaning of the *Abhidharmakośa*,
no longer engaged in face-to-face debate with him.
The Dharma Master said, "I am now old; do as you wish. In the past, when I composed a treatise to refute the doctrines of the *Vibhāṣā*, I did not debate and resolve the matter in your presence."
Now that you are composing this treatise, why must you call upon me, a person of wisdom?
You should know for yourself what is right and wrong.
Since the Dharma Master has thoroughly mastered the meanings of all eighteen schools, [you need not seek my counsel].
Those who have a refined understanding of the Hīnayāna yet cling to it will,
because of this, lack faith in the Mahāyāna,
asserting that the Mahāyāna was not taught by the Buddha.
When Dharma Master Asaṅga saw that this younger brother was more intelligent than others, possessed profound and extensive understanding, and had mastered both Buddhist and non-Buddhist teachings,
he feared that he might compose a treatise to destroy the Mahāyāna.
The Dharma Master Asaṅga was residing in the country of Puruṣapura.
He dispatched a messenger to the country of Ayodhyā to inform Vasubandhu, saying:
"I am now critically ill; you should come at once."
Vasubandhu then accompanied the messenger back to his own country to meet his elder brother and inquire about the origin of his illness.
His brother replied, "I now have a grave illness of the mind, which has arisen because of you."
Maitreya asked again, "What is the reason for this?
His elder brother replied, "You do not believe in the Mahāyāna and constantly harbor slander toward it.
Because of these evil karmic actions, you will surely sink forever into the evil realms."
"I am now so afflicted by grief that my life will not be preserved.
Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu was struck with alarm and fear, and immediately requested his elder brother to explain the Mahāyāna for him.
His brother then briefly expounded the essential meaning of the Mahāyāna.
The Dharma Master was intelligent, with a depth of understanding that varied;
at this very moment, he realized the principles of the Mahāyāna,
which should transcend those of the Hīnayāna.
Thereupon, he studied the Mahāyāna doctrines extensively under his elder brother.
Later, he attained complete mastery of everything his brother had understood; his comprehension of the meaning was clear and his contemplation was lucid.
From beginning to end, everything was in accord with principle, without any contradiction.
This is the first proof that the Hīnayāna is a loss and the Mahāyāna is a gain.
If there were no Mahāyāna, there would be no path or fruit of the Three Vehicles.
Previously, you slandered the Mahāyāna and failed to give rise to faith or joy.
Fearing that this karmic offense would inevitably lead him to the evil realms,
he deeply reproached himself, wishing to repent for his past transgressions.
He went to his elder brother’s place and recounted his delusions and errors, declaring his desire to perform repentance.
Not knowing by what means he might first be freed from his transgressions,
he said, "In the past, it was because of my tongue that I gave rise to slander;
I shall now cut out my tongue to atone for this sin."
The elder brother said, "Even if you were to cut out a thousand tongues, you could not extinguish this sin.
If you wish to extinguish this sin, you must employ further skillful means.
The Dharma Master then requested his brother to explain the skillful means for extinguishing the sin.
The elder brother said, "Your tongue has been capable of skillfully slandering the Mahāyāna.
If you wish to extinguish this transgression, you must skillfully explain the Mahāyāna.
After the Dharma Master Asaṅga had passed away...
Only then did Vasubandhu compose Mahāyāna treatises to explain various Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the Avataṃsaka, the Nirvāṇa,
the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka, the Prajñāpāramitā, the Vimalakīrti, and the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda.
All the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras were composed by this Dharma Master.

Furthermore, he composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) and commentaries on various Mahāyāna treatises, such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Ratnatrayaparīkṣā*, and the *Amṛtadvāra*.
Whatever the Dharma Master has composed is so refined and subtle in both its phrasing and meaning that all who see or hear it cannot fail to believe in and seek it. Thus,
among those who study the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna in India and other border regions, [it is universally esteemed].
They all took what the Dharma Master had composed as their fundamental texts for study.
When masters of other schools and non-Buddhist traditions heard the Dharma Master’s name, none failed to be awed and submit.
He passed away in the kingdom of Āyodhyā at the age of eighty.
Although his traces remained in the realm of ordinary beings, in principle he was truly inconceivable.

Up to this point, the records concerning the brothers Vasubandhu and others have been concluded; hereafter, the records concerning the Tripiṭaka Ācārya—his travels from the Imperial City to Guangzhou in the east, his retranslation of various Mahāyāna treatises, and his subsequent passing—are transmitted for future generations.
